nodes.heading: Company Overview
nodes.start_phrase: We were incorporated in Delaware in 1919 and reincorporated in North Carolina in 1986.
nodes.summary:
- Forward-looking statements disclaimer: The 10-K includes statements about future performance identified by terms like “anticipate,” “expect,” “plan,” etc., made under the PSLRA. These are based on current information and involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Readers are cautioned not to rely unduly, and the company undertakes no duty to update. Key risk references: Item 1A (Risk Factors) and Item 7 (MD&A – Our Business Risks).
- Part I, Item 1 – Business: Defines “we,” “us,” “our,” “PepsiCo,” and notes a Glossary in Item 7.
- Company overview: Incorporated in Delaware in 1919; reincorporated in North Carolina in 1986. PepsiCo is a leading global beverage and convenient foods company with a complementary brand portfolio, including Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Gatorade, Pepsi-Cola, Mountain Dew, Quaker, and SodaStream. Products are made, marketed, distributed, and sold through company operations and third parties (authorized bottlers, contract manufacturers, etc.) in more than 200 countries and territories.
- Operations and reportable segments: The company is organized into seven divisions; the excerpt lists five:
  - Frito-Lay North America (FLNA): branded convenient foods in the U.S. and Canada.
  - Quaker Foods North America (QFNA): cereals, rice, pasta, and other branded foods in the U.S. and Canada.
  - PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA): beverages in the U.S. and Canada.
  - Latin America (LatAm): beverages and convenient foods in Latin America.
  - Europe: beverages and convenient foods in Europe.

nodes.title: Our Operations
nodes.heading: Our Operations
nodes.start_phrase: We are or ganized into seven reportable segments (also referred to as divisions), as follows:
nodes.summary:
- Forward-looking statements: The report outlines that it contains statements about future performance under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, identifies common forward-looking terms, emphasizes associated risks and uncertainties, references Item 1A (Risk Factors) and Item 7 (MD&A) for details, cautions investors, and disclaims any obligation to update such statements.
- Company overview: PepsiCo, Inc. (incorporated in Delaware in 1919; reincorporated in North Carolina in 1986) is a global beverage and convenient foods company operating in 200+ countries and territories, with a complementary brand portfolio including Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Gatorade, Pepsi-Cola, Mountain Dew, Quaker and SodaStream. Operations involve company facilities, authorized bottlers, contract manufacturers and other third parties. Certain terms are defined in a glossary in Item 7.
- Reportable segments: Seven divisions are identified—Frito-Lay North America (FLNA); Quaker Foods North America (QFNA); PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA); Latin America (LatAm); Europe; Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA); and Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China Region (APAC).
- FLNA: Produces and sells branded convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Fritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Tostitos, branded dips) to independent distributors and retailers; includes the Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads joint venture with Strauss Group.
- QFNA: Produces and sells branded cereals, rice, pasta and other foods (e.g., Cap’n Crunch, Life, Pearl Milling Company syrups/mixes, Quaker Chewy, grits, oatmeal, rice cakes, Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni) to independent distributors and retailers.
- PBNA: Produces and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups and finished goods (e.g., Aquafina, Diet Mountain Dew, Diet Pepsi, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, Propel); operates bottling plants and distribution; sells to independent distributors/retailers and to authorized/independent bottlers. Includes joint ventures for ready-to-drink tea and coffee with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks; manufactures/distributes licensed brands from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray; began distributing Hard MTN Dew (manufactured/owned by Boston Beer) in 2022. In 1Q22, completed the Juice Transaction with PAI Partners, creating Tropicana Brands Group (TBG) with PepsiCo retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest; PepsiCo serves as exclusive U.S. distributor for TBG’s chilled DSD to small-format and foodservice; cross-referenced to Note 13.
- Latin America (intro): Produces and sells convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos, Quaker-branded foods) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Diet 7UP, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, San Carlos, Toddy), with sales to authorized/independent bottlers, independent distributors and retailers.

nodes.title: Our Operations - Introduction

nodes.summary: This section introduces the company’s organizational structure of seven reportable segments (divisions) and their scopes: Frito-Lay North America (FLNA) for branded convenient foods in the U.S. and Canada; Quaker Foods North America (QFNA) for branded convenient foods including cereal, rice, pasta and other foods in the U.S. and Canada; PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA) for beverages in the U.S. and Canada; Latin America (LatAm) for all beverage and convenient food businesses in Latin America; Europe for all beverage and convenient food businesses in Europe; Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA) for all beverage and convenient food businesses across those regions; and Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China Region (APAC) for all beverage and convenient food businesses across Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and the China region.

nodes.title: Frito-Lay North America
nodes.heading: Frito-Lay North America
nodes.start_phrase: Either independentl y or in conjunction with third parties, FLNA makes, markets, distributes and sells branded convenient foods.
nodes.summary:
- Defines two international segments: AMESA (Africa, Middle East and South Asia) and APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China region), covering both beverage and convenient foods.
- Describes Frito-Lay North America (FLNA): manufactures and sells branded convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Fritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Tostitos) primarily through independent distributors and retailers; includes the Sabra refrigerated dips JV with Strauss Group.
- Describes Quaker Foods North America (QFNA): produces cereals, rice, pasta, and other branded foods (e.g., Cap’n Crunch, Life, Pearl Milling Company, Quaker oatmeal/grits/chewy bars/rice cakes/Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni) sold via independent distributors and retailers.
- Describes PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA): makes and sells concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished beverages (e.g., Aquafina, Pepsi, Diet Pepsi, Mountain Dew/Diet, Gatorade/Zero, Propel); operates bottling plants and distribution; sells through independent distributors/retailers and authorized/independent bottlers.
- Highlights PBNA partnerships and licenses: RTD tea/coffee JVs with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks; licenses from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray.
- Notes 2022 initiatives: began distributing Hard MTN Dew (manufactured/owned by Boston Beer Company); executed the “Juice Transaction” selling Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners, forming Tropicana Brands Group (TBG) with a 39% noncontrolling interest; PepsiCo is exclusive U.S. distributor for TBG brands in small-format and foodservice via chilled DSD.
- Describes Latin America (LatAm): produces and sells convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos, Quaker-branded) and beverages (e.g., 7UP/Diet, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi/Pepsi Black, San Carlos, Toddy) through authorized/independent bottlers, distributors, and retailers.

nodes.title: Quaker Foods North America
nodes.heading: Quaker Foods North America
nodes.start_phrase: Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, QFNA makes, markets, distributes and sells branded convenient foods, which include cereals, rice, pasta and other branded products.
nodes.summary:
- Defines two international segments: AMESA (Africa, Middle East and South Asia) and APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China region), covering both beverages and convenient foods in those geographies.
- Describes Frito-Lay North America (FLNA): manufactures and sells branded convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Fritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Tostitos, branded dips), sold to independent distributors and retailers; includes a joint venture with Strauss Group for Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads.
- Describes Quaker Foods North America (QFNA): produces cereals and other convenient foods (e.g., Cap’n Crunch, Life, Pearl Milling Company, Quaker oatmeal/grits/rice cakes/Chewy/Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni), sold to independent distributors and retailers.
- Details PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA): makes and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods (e.g., Aquafina, Pepsi, Diet Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Diet Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Propel); operates bottling and distribution, sells directly and via authorized/independent bottlers; joint ventures for ready-to-drink tea (Unilever/Lipton) and coffee (Starbucks); licenses certain brands from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray; began distributing Hard MTN Dew (Boston Beer) in 2022; executed the 2022 Juice Transaction selling Tropicana, Naked and other select juice brands to PAI Partners, retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in Tropicana Brands Group and serving as exclusive U.S. distributor to small-format and foodservice customers via chilled DSD.
- Outlines Latin America (LatAm): produces and sells convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos, Quaker-branded foods) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Diet 7UP, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, San Carlos, Toddy), distributed through authorized/independent bottlers, independent distributors, and retailers.

nodes.title: PepsiCo Beverages North America
nodes.heading: PepsiCo Beverages North America
nodes.start_phrase: Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, PBNA makes, markets and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups and finished goods under various beverage brands including Aquafina, Diet Mountain Dew, Diet Pepsi, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Mountain Dew, Pepsi and Propel.
nodes.summary:
Overview of PepsiCo’s segment structure and activities:
- Defines AMESA (Africa, Middle East and South Asia) and APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China Region) segments.
- Details Frito-Lay North America (FLNA) operations: manufacturing, marketing, distribution and sales of snack brands (Cheetos, Doritos, Fritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Tostitos, branded dips) primarily through independent distributors and retailers; includes Sabra refrigerated dips JV with Strauss Group.
- Details Quaker Foods North America (QFNA): cereals and convenient foods (Cap’n Crunch, Life, Pearl Milling Company, Quaker oatmeal/grits/granola bars/rice cakes/Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni) sold via independent distributors and retailers.
- Details PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA): concentrates, fountain syrups and finished beverages (Aquafina, Pepsi, Diet Pepsi, Mountain Dew/Diet, Gatorade/Gatorade Zero, Propel); owns bottling and distribution; sells to independent distributors/retailers and to authorized/independent bottlers. Includes RTD tea/coffee JVs with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks; licenses brands from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes), and juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray. Began distributing Hard MTN Dew (Boston Beer Company) in 2022. Completed 2022 sale of Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners, retaining 39% in Tropicana Brands Group (TBG) operating in North America and Europe; PepsiCo is exclusive U.S. distributor to small-format and foodservice customers via chilled DSD.
- Details Latin America (LatAm): snack brands (Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos, Quaker foods) and beverage brands (7UP/Diet 7UP, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi/Pepsi Black, San Carlos, Toddy) sold through authorized/independent bottlers, independent distributors and retailers.
- Emphasizes multi-channel distribution models across segments, including direct-store-delivery (DSD), independent distributors, retailers and bottler networks.

nodes.title: Latin America
nodes.heading: Latin America
nodes.start_phrase: Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, LatAm makes, markets, distributes and sells a number of convenient food brands including Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador , Lay’s, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas and Tostitos, as well as many Quaker -branded convenient foods .
nodes.summary:
- Overview of PepsiCo’s global operating segments and their scope: FLNA, QFNA, PBNA, Latin America, Europe, Africa/Middle East/South Asia (AMESA), and Asia Pacific/Australia & New Zealand/China (APAC).
- FLNA: U.S. snack portfolio (Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Ruffles, Fritos, Tostitos, branded dips); joint venture with Strauss Group for Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads; sales to independent distributors and retailers.
- QFNA: Branded convenient foods (Quaker oatmeal, grits, rice cakes, Simply Granola; Cap’n Crunch, Life; Pearl Milling Company syrups and mixes; Quaker Chewy; Rice-A-Roni); sales to independent distributors and retailers.
- PBNA: Beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods (Pepsi, Diet Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Diet Mountain Dew, Aquafina, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Propel); own bottling and distribution plus sales to authorized/independent bottlers; RTD tea and coffee via JVs with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks; licenses for Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes (from Keurig Dr Pepper) and certain Dole/Ocean Spray juice brands; began distributing Hard MTN Dew (Boston Beer) in 2022; 2022 sale of Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners with a retained 39% stake in Tropicana Brands Group (TBG) and U.S. chilled DSD exclusivity for small-format and foodservice.
- Latin America: Snack brands (Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos) and Quaker foods; beverages (7UP, Diet 7UP, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, San Carlos, Toddy); sales via authorized/independent bottlers, distributors, and retailers; RTD tea JV with Unilever (Lipton).
- Europe: Snacks (Lay’s, Walkers, Doritos, Cheetos, Ruffles) and Quaker foods via consolidated and noncontrolled affiliates; beverages (7UP, Diet Pepsi, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Max, Lubimy Sad) with a mix of own bottling and third-party bottlers; SodaStream makers and related products; dairy brands (Agusha, Chudo, Domik v Derevne); RTD tea JV with Unilever; 2022 TBG juice transaction noted.
- AMESA: Snacks (Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, Sasko, Spekko, White Star) and Quaker foods via consolidated and noncontrolled affiliates; beverages (7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi); mix of own bottling and third-party networks; RTD tea JV with Unilever.
- APAC: Snacks (BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Smith’s) and Quaker foods via consolidated and noncontrolled affiliates; beverages (7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, Sting); RTD tea JV with Unilever.
- Distribution: Multi-channel model using direct-store-delivery (DSD), customer warehouse, distributor networks, and e-commerce; route-to-market tailored by customer needs, product characteristics, and local trade practices.

nodes.title: Our Distribution Network
nodes.heading: Our Distribution Network
nodes.start_phrase: Our products are primarily brought to market through DSD, customer warehouse and distributor networks and are also sold directly to consumers through e-commerce platforms and retailers.
nodes.summary:
- Regional business overviews:
  - Europe: Produces and sells convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Walkers, Quaker) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Diet Pepsi, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Max); operates via consolidated businesses and noncontrolled affiliates; uses authorized/independent bottlers and, in some markets, its own bottling and distribution; includes SodaStream; sells dairy products (Agusha, Chudo, Domik v Derevne); participates in a Lipton RTD tea JV with Unilever; sold Tropicana, Naked, and select juice brands to PAI Partners in 2022 while retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in TBG across North America and Europe.
  - Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA): Offers convenient foods (e.g., Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, Sasko, Spekko, White Star, Quaker) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi); uses bottlers, independent distributors/retailers, and in some markets its own bottling; participates in the Lipton RTD tea JV.
  - Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China (APAC): Offers convenient foods (e.g., BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Smith’s, Quaker) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, Sting); relies on authorized/independent bottlers and third-party partners; participates in the Lipton RTD tea JV.

- Distribution network:
  - Direct-Store-Delivery (DSD): Direct delivery to retail with in-store merchandising, suited to frequently restocked, promotion-responsive products.
  - Customer warehouse: Shipments from company/third-party facilities to customer warehouses, better for less fragile, lower-turnover items.
  - Distributor networks: Third-party distributors expand reach, including foodservice and vending channels to restaurants, businesses, schools, and stadiums.

- Ingredients, packaging, and supplies:
  - Key ingredients: Aspartame, corn/corn sweeteners, flavorings, flour, juice concentrates, oats, potatoes, raw milk, rice, seasonings, sucralose, sugar, vegetable/essential oils, wheat, and water.
  - Packaging: PET and polypropylene resins, film packaging, aluminum, glass, closures, cardboard, paperboard; integration of recyclability and increased recycled content (including recycled PET).
  - Energy and logistics: Fuel, electricity, natural gas critical for operations and distribution.

- Sourcing and risk management:
  - Procurement largely in open markets with exposure managed via fixed-price contracts, purchase orders, pricing agreements, and derivatives (swaps, futures).
  - Supply risk mitigation through multi-geo and multi-supplier strategies.
  - Ongoing sustainability initiatives: advancing sustainable farming practices and expanding globally.
  - 2022–2023 headwinds: Higher commodity, packaging, and input costs; supply constraints tied to the Ukraine conflict, COVID-19, inflation, adverse weather, supply chain disruptions, and labor shortages.

nodes.title: Ingredients and Other Supplies

- Outlines PepsiCo’s primary go-to-market and distribution models: Direct-Store-Delivery (DSD) for high-visibility, fast-turn items; customer warehouse delivery for less fragile, lower-turn products; third-party distributor networks (including foodservice and vending); and growing direct-to-consumer e-commerce.

nodes.title: Our Brands and Intellectual Property Rights
nodes.heading: Our Brands and Intellectual Pr operty Rights
nodes.start_phrase: We own numerous valuable trademark s which are essential to our worldwide businesses, including Agusha, Amp Energy, Aquafina, Aquafina Flavorsplash, Arto Lifewtr , Baja Blast, BaiCaoW ei, Bare, Bokomo, bubly ,

nodes.title: Seasonality
nodes.heading: Seasonality
nodes.start_phrase: Our businesses are affected by seasona l variations.
nodes.summary:
- Extensive overview of brands and intellectual property: large global trademark portfolio across beverages and convenient foods; emphasis on proper trademark use, broad licensing for bottlers, joint ventures, and retail merchandise; ownership/licensing of patents covering products, packaging, processes, and equipment.
- Key brand and partnership moves: distribution of Celsius energy drinks and select Keurig Dr Pepper brands (e.g., Dr Pepper in certain markets, Crush, Schweppes); joint ventures with rights to brands such as Lipton, Sabra, and Starbucks; 2022 sale of Tropicana, Naked and other juice brands to PAI Partners with PepsiCo retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in TBG and serving as exclusive U.S. distributor for TBG’s chilled DSD in small-format and foodservice; launch of Hard MTN Dew via trademark license to Boston Beer Company with PepsiCo as distributor.
- Seasonality: beverage and snack sales peak in Q3 and are lowest in Q1; overall seasonality not material to consolidated financial results.
- Customer base and routes to market: diverse set of customers including wholesalers, foodservice, mass and dollar retailers, club, convenience, drug, e-commerce, and independent bottlers; exclusive territorial bottling contracts with rights to charge for concentrate/finished goods and Aquafina royalties; defined manufacturing standards and geographic distribution rights.
- Trade and marketing investments: detailed programs for distributors/retailers (volume rebates, placement fees, promotions, displays) and annual bottler funding (consumer incentives, advertising/media support, new product support, vending/cooler placement).
- Retail landscape dynamics: increased retailer consolidation, growth of e-commerce and direct-to-consumer models, omnichannel integration, and international expansion of hard discounters heighten the importance of major customers.
- Customer concentration: Walmart (including Sam’s Club) represented ~14% of 2022 consolidated net revenue; loss of Walmart would materially adversely affect FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA.
- Competitive environment: intense competition from global, regional, local, private label, and micro-brand players; primary beverage competitor is The Coca-Cola Company; other notable competitors include Campbell, Conagra, Hormel, Kellogg, Keurig Dr Pepper, Kraft Heinz, Link Snacks, Mondelēz, Monster, Nestlé, Red Bull, and Utz.
- Market position: strong leadership in many snack categories; in 2022 U.S. liquid refreshment beverages, PepsiCo had ~20% retail share vs. Coca-Cola’s ~21%; Coca-Cola holds CSD share advantages in many markets outside the U.S.

nodes.title: Our Customers
nodes.heading: Our Customers
nodes.start_phrase: Our custom ers inclu de wholesale and other distributors, foodservice customers, grocery stores, drug stores, convenience stores, discount/dollar stores, mass merchandisers, membership stores, hard discounters, e-commerce retailers and authorized independent bottlers , among others.
nodes.summary:
- Customer base spans wholesale and other distributors, foodservice, grocery, drug and convenience stores, discount/dollar and mass merchandisers, membership clubs, hard discounters, e-commerce retailers, and authorized independent bottlers.
- Independent bottlers typically receive exclusive territorial rights to manufacture and/or distribute certain trademarked beverages; the company sells them concentrate/finished goods, charges Aquafina royalties, and prescribes manufacturing standards.
- The company funds trade and consumer programs: for distributors/retailers via volume rebates, placement fees, promotions and displays; for bottlers via annually negotiated “bottler funding” supporting consumer incentives, advertising/media, new product launches (including point-of-purchase and placement fees), and vending/cooler equipment deployment; program mix changes annually.
- Retail landscape shifts—retailer consolidation, growth of e-commerce and mobile commerce (including subscriptions and DTC), omnichannel integration, expansion of hard discounters, and macroeconomic conditions—heighten reliance on major customers.
- Walmart (including Sam’s Club) accounted for ~14% of 2022 consolidated net revenue across divisions (including concentrate sold to bottlers for Walmart-bound finished goods); losing Walmart would materially adversely affect FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA.
- Competitive environment is intense across beverages and convenient foods, with competition from global, regional, local, private-label, and e-commerce-driven microbrands; primary beverage competitor is The Coca-Cola Company.
- Other notable competitors include Campbell Soup, Conagra, Hormel, Kellogg, Keurig Dr Pepper, Kraft Heinz, Link Snacks, Mondelēz, Monster, Nestlé, Red Bull, and Utz.
- The company holds leading positions in many convenient food categories; in 2022 it represented ~20% of U.S. liquid refreshment beverage retail sales (measured channels) vs. Coca-Cola at ~21%; Coca-Cola has a strong CSD share advantage in many non-U.S. markets.

nodes.title: Our Competition
nodes.heading: Our Competition
nodes.start_phrase: Our beverage and convenient food products are in highly competitive categori es and markets and compete against products of international beverage and convenient food companies that, like us, operate in multiple geographies,
nodes.summary:
- Customers and distribution: Broad customer base spanning wholesalers, distributors, foodservice, grocery, drug, convenience, discount/dollar, mass merchandisers, membership clubs, hard discounters, e-commerce, and authorized independent bottlers. Independent bottlers typically have exclusive territorial contracts; the company charges for concentrate, finished goods, and Aquafina royalties, specifies manufacturing processes, and grants distribution rights.

- Trade and bottler incentives: Financial incentives to drive distribution and promotion, including volume-based rebates, placement fees, promotions, and displays for distributors/retailers. Annual “bottler funding” supports consumer incentives, advertising/media, new product support (materials, placement fees, media), and vending/cooler equipment placement; program types vary year to year.

- Retail landscape and customer concentration: Ongoing consolidation, growth of e-commerce and subscriptions, omnichannel integration, international expansion of hard discounters, and macroeconomic factors heighten reliance on major customers. Walmart (including Sam’s Club) represented about 14% of 2022 consolidated net revenue; loss of this customer would materially adversely affect the FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA divisions.

- Competitive environment: Intense competition from global, regional, local, private label, and micro brands (including DTC/e-commerce). Primary beverage competitor is The Coca-Cola Company; other notable competitors include Campbell Soup, Conagra, Hormel, Kellogg, Keurig Dr Pepper, Kraft Heinz, Link Snacks, Mondelēz, Monster, Nestlé, Red Bull, and Utz. In 2022, the company and Coca-Cola held approximately 20% and 21% U.S. liquid refreshment beverage retail sales share, respectively; Coca-Cola has significant CSD share outside the U.S.

- Competitive factors and success drivers: Competition on brand strength and loyalty, taste, price/value, quality, variety, innovation, distribution, advertising/marketing (including digital), packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to health/wellness, sustainability, and e-commerce trends. Success depends on effective promotion, new product launches and reformulations, production efficiency, incorporation of technology/digital tools, impactful advertising, packaging and pricing, new vending/dispensing equipment, and robust brand/trademark protection. The company cites brand strength, innovation, marketing, product quality, and distribution flexibility as advantages.

- Research and development focus: Global innovation aimed at growth and meeting customer/consumer needs, including new technologies, ingredients, flavors, and substrates; manufacturing improvements to reduce cost and environmental footprint; reformulations to lower added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat; expanded offerings with functional ingredients and positive nutrition (whole grains, fruits/vegetables, dairy, protein, fiber, micronutrients, hydration); sustainable packaging (reduced plastic; recyclable/compostable/biodegradable options); marketing/merchandising/dispensing equipment; “beyond the bottle” (e.g., SodaStream); technology and digitalization (AI, data analytics) for insights and research; strengthened omnichannel and e-commerce; environmental impact reduction (water use, agricultural practices, operational footprint). Research centers located in Brazil, China, India, Ireland, Mexico, Russia, South Africa, the U.K., and the U.S.

- Regulatory matters: Business activities across the product lifecycle and employment/data protection are subject to extensive U.S. and international laws and regulations. U.S. examples include the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act and state food safety laws, the Food Safety Modernization Act, and the Occupational Safety and Health Act and related state workplace health regulations.

nodes.title: Research and Development
nodes.heading: Resear ch and Development
nodes.start_phrase: We engage in a variety of research and development activities and invest in innovation globally with the goal of meeting the needs of our custom ers and consumers and accelerating growth.
nodes.summary:
- Competitive landscape: Beverage and convenient foods compete on brand strength, taste, price/value, quality, variety, innovation, distribution reach, advertising/marketing (including digital), packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to consumer trends (health/wellness, sustainability, e-commerce). Success factors include effective promotion and reformulation, efficient production, adoption of technology/digital tools, impactful advertising and pricing, new vending/dispensing equipment, and strong brand/trademark protection. The company cites brand strength, innovation, marketing, product quality, and a flexible distribution network as key advantages.

- Research and development focus: Global innovation to meet customer/consumer needs and drive growth, including:
  - New technologies, ingredients, flavors, and substrates to create consumer-preferred products.
  - Manufacturing process improvements to lower cost and environmental footprint.
  - Reformulations reducing added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat.
  - Expanding offerings with functional ingredients and positive nutrition (whole grains, fruits/vegetables, dairy, protein, fiber, micronutrients, hydration).
  - Sustainable packaging innovations (reduced plastic; recyclable/compostable/biodegradable options) and new package designs.
  - Development of marketing, merchandising, and dispensing equipment.
  - “Beyond the bottle” expansion, including SodaStream innovation.
  - Technology and digitalization (AI and data analytics) to enhance insights and research; strengthening omnichannel, especially e-commerce.
  - Environmental initiatives across the value chain, including reduced water use and sustainable agricultural practices.
  - Global R&D centers in Brazil, China, India, Ireland, Mexico, Russia, South Africa, the U.K., and the U.S., leveraging consumer insights, food science, and engineering.

- Regulatory matters: Operations across product lifecycle and employment practices are subject to extensive laws and regulations in the U.S. and in 200+ countries/territories. Areas include production, storage, distribution, sales, display, advertising, marketing, labeling, content, quality, safety, transportation, packaging, disposal, recycling, product use, occupational health and safety, and data protection. U.S. frameworks cited include the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, Food Safety Modernization Act, and Occupational Safety and Health Act, along with relevant state laws. The company’s policy is to comply with applicable laws globally.

nodes.title: Regulatory Matters
nodes.heading: Regulatory Matters
nodes.start_phrase: The conduct of our businesses, including the production, storage, distribution, sale, display , advertising, marketing, labeling, content, quality , safety, transportation, packaging, disposal, recycling and use of our products,
nodes.summary:
- Competitive landscape: how PepsiCo competes in beverages and convenient foods through brand strength, taste, price/value, quality, product variety and innovation, distribution, advertising/marketing (including digital), packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to health, wellness, sustainability, and e-commerce trends; key success drivers include effective promotion, new product launches and reformulations, production efficiency, technology/digital adoption, pricing/packaging, equipment, and brand/trademark protection.

- Research and development: global innovation focus on consumer‑preferred products via new technologies, ingredients, flavors and substrates; manufacturing process improvements to lower cost and environmental footprint; nutrition enhancements (reducing added sugars, sodium, saturated fat) and adding functional/positive nutrition; sustainable packaging (less plastic, recyclable/compostable/biodegradable); marketing/merchandising/dispensing equipment; “beyond the bottle” growth including SodaStream; investments in technology and digitalization (AI, data analytics), omnichannel/e‑commerce capabilities; environmental impact reductions across operations and agriculture; global R&D centers in multiple countries.

- Regulatory environment: extensive compliance requirements across production, labeling, marketing, safety, employment, data privacy, transportation, packaging, disposal/recycling in the U.S. and 200+ other jurisdictions; U.S. laws cited include FDA/FSMA, OSHA, environmental statutes, FTC/Lanham, antitrust (Robinson‑Patman, Clayton), labor (EEO, NLRA, FLSA), alcohol, privacy (CCPA/CPRA), trade/customs, school sales, ingredient rules, supply chain transparency, FCPA, sanctions, and California Proposition 65; non‑U.S. laws include food safety, trade/tariffs, supply chain (UK Modern Slavery Act), OSH, competition, anti‑corruption (UK Bribery Act), data privacy (GDPR); reliance on legal/compliance programs and counsel.

- Public policy impacts: existing and proposed beverage/sugar taxes with varying structures; product labeling/warning and marketing/sales restrictions (including age and location limits); packaging and recycling regulations such as deposit return systems, extended producer responsibility, and restrictions/bans on single‑use plastics and PFAS‑containing packaging.

- Environmental compliance and ESG: subject to U.S. and international environmental laws (Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, CERCLA, RCRA, etc.); ongoing spend for compliance and to meet sustainability goals; potential for increased costs from evolving climate, water, and ESG reporting rules; environmental remediation and indemnification obligations not expected to be material.

- Human capital: importance of attracting, developing, and retaining talent; Board and committee oversight of culture, DEI, pay equity, health and safety, training/development, and compensation/benefits; workforce of ~315,000 (132,000 U.S.), collective bargaining relationships; commitment to an injury‑free workplace with safety technologies (telematics, distracted‑driving, ergonomics, machine safety); continued COVID‑19 protections for frontline associates.

nodes.title: Human Capital
nodes.heading: Human Capital
nodes.start_phrase: PepsiCo believes that human capital management, including attracting, developing and retaining a high quality workforce, is critical to our long-term success.
nodes.summary:
- Expanding regulatory landscape on packaging and waste, including container return mandates, extended producer responsibility (EPR), and restrictions/bans on single-use plastics and PFAS-containing packaging; potential for more stringent future rules.
- Compliance with U.S. and international environmental laws (e.g., Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, CERCLA, RCRA) covering water use/treatment, wastewater discharge, air emissions, and waste handling; internal global compliance programs in place.
- Ongoing and anticipated expenditures to meet environmental requirements and sustainability goals; costs have not been material to date but could adversely affect financial performance if requirements change.
- Environmental remediation and indemnification obligations arise from normal operations and historical activities; currently not expected to be material to capital expenditures, earnings, or competitive position.
- Recognition that ESG and climate concerns may drive new mandates on emissions reductions, water use limits, and expanded mandatory ESG reporting.
- Human capital management overseen by the Board and its committees, covering culture, diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), pay equity, health and safety, training and development, and compensation/benefits.
- Workforce details: approximately 315,000 employees globally (about 132,000 in the U.S.); numerous collective bargaining agreements; generally good labor relations.
- Safety and wellbeing focus: injury prevention, fleet telematics and distracted-driving technologies, ergonomic and machine-safety measures; continued COVID-19 protocols (PPE, testing) for frontline workers; support and humanitarian aid for associates in Ukraine.
- DEI metrics: ~27% female global workforce; ~44% female in management; in the U.S., ~48% racially/ethnically diverse workforce and ~33% racially/ethnically diverse in managerial roles; leadership team includes seven diverse executives reporting to the CEO.
- Employee development: broad training programs, mentoring, career development, and the PEP U Degreed online learning platform; over 1 million training hours completed in 2022.
- Investor information: SEC filings available on the SEC website and PepsiCo’s website; company uses multiple channels (filings, press releases, calls, webcasts, website) for material disclosures; website information may be material but is not incorporated by reference; channels may change.
- Transition to Item 1A Risk Factors, noting that identified and potential risks could materially affect business and securities, and that the list is not exhaustive.

Business Risks

nodes.title: Risks associated with the deadly conflict in Ukraine
nodes.heading: Risks associated with the deadly conflict in Ukraine
nodes.start_phrase: The deadly conflict in Ukraine has continued to result in worldwide geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty and certain of our opera tions in Ukraine remain suspended.
nodes.summary:
- Describes business risks, emphasizing the ongoing impacts of the Ukraine conflict: suspended operations in Ukraine; heightened geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty; commodity price volatility; supply chain and logistics disruptions; increased cyber/IT risks; employee safety concerns; labor shortages; Russian ruble volatility; constrained access to credit and banking services (including working capital); higher transportation, energy, packaging and raw material costs; environmental, health and safety challenges at facilities; additional sanctions/export controls and fund transfer restrictions; potential asset losses or impairments; and adverse effects on sustainability goals and global demand.

- Explains risk of reduced future demand tied to the company’s ability to innovate and respond to evolving consumer preferences and channels (e-commerce and online-to-offline), pricing and product quality expectations, environmental concerns about packaging (e.g., single-use plastics), perceptions of nutrition and ingredient origin (including from third-party studies), and shifts due to pandemics/epidemics. Highlights the influence of brand image, marketing effectiveness, digital engagement and social media, and responses to political/social issues. Notes that misreading trends or underinvesting (including in data analytics) can lead to lower demand, inventory write-offs, and weakened competitive/financial position. Warns that natural disasters, pandemics, and other uncontrollable events can disrupt supply, reduce product availability, and dampen demand if crisis management is ineffective.

- Identifies reputation and brand image risk: sales depend on maintaining a positive global reputation, which can be damaged by failures by the company or its partners to uphold ethical standards and ESG practices, including compliance with human rights and child labor laws and commitments to diversity, equity and inclusion.

nodes.title: Reduction in future demand for our products would adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Reduction in future demand for our products would adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Demand for our products depends in part on our ability to innovate and anticipate and effectively respond to shifts in consumer trends and preferenc es, including the types of products our consumers want and how they browse for, purchase and consume them.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines key business risks. It highlights extensive impacts from the conflict in Ukraine, including suspended operations, geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty, supply chain and cyber disruptions, employee safety risks, labor shortages, ruble volatility, restricted access to credit and banking services, rising costs for transportation, energy, packaging and raw materials, evolving sanctions/export controls, potential asset losses or impairments, and possible setbacks to sustainability goals and product demand. It details risks of reduced future demand driven by failure to innovate or anticipate shifting consumer preferences across channels (including e-commerce), concerns about packaging and environmental impact (e.g., plastics), perceptions of nutrition/ingredient origin influenced by third-party studies, pricing and product quality, pandemic-driven demand shifts, brand image and marketing effectiveness, digital engagement, and reactions to social/political issues that may spur boycotts; it also notes the potential for inventory write-offs and operational disruptions from natural disasters and disease outbreaks if crisis management is ineffective. Finally, it underscores reputational risk, where failures by the company or its partners to uphold strong ethical, business, and ESG standards—covering areas like human rights, child labor, diversity, and equity—can damage brand image and adversely affect the business.

nodes.title: Damage to our reputation or brand image can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Damage to our reputation or brand image can adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Maintaining a positive reputation globally is critical to selling our products.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on Business Risks, emphasizing how external events and internal execution can adversely affect operations, demand, and financial performance.
- Ukraine conflict risks: suspended operations in parts of Ukraine; heightened geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty; volatile commodity markets; supply chain disruptions; increased cyber risk; employee safety concerns; business disruptions (including labor shortages); ruble volatility; restricted access to credit and banking services (e.g., working capital); higher transportation, energy, packaging, and raw material costs; environmental, health and safety risks in maintaining facilities; sanctions and export controls (including fund transfer restrictions); potential asset loss or impairments; negative impacts on demand and sustainability goals.
- Demand volatility: need to anticipate and respond to shifting consumer preferences across channels (e-commerce, online-to-offline), pricing, product quality, packaging sustainability (e.g., plastics), nutrition/health and ingredient-origin concerns (including from third-party studies), and pandemic-driven behavior changes; dependence on brand image, effective advertising/marketing, digital engagement and social media; risks from public responses to political/social issues or catastrophic events; failure to invest in data analytics or make the right strategic choices can reduce demand, cause inventory write-offs, and erode competitiveness; natural disasters/pandemics can disrupt supply and depress demand if crisis plans are ineffective.
- Reputation/brand image: vulnerability to perceived or actual failures in ethics and ESG (human rights, child labor, DEI, workplace conditions, employee health/safety); not meeting ESG goals (nutrition profile, packaging, water, environmental impact); handling of health concerns (including alcoholic beverages distributed); R&D outcomes; product quality/safety issues and recalls; compliance with laws and regulations; perceptions of advertising, sponsorships, social media use, and responses to social/political events; inability to counter negative commentary can reduce demand.
- Product quality and safety: recalls due to mislabeling, misbranding, spoilage, undeclared allergens, adulteration, or contamination (including at joint ventures); costs from recalls, destroyed inventory, lost sales, production/delivery disruptions, fines/judgments, and reputational harm; expanding into new categories (e.g., alcohol) increases exposure; inadequate oversight may trigger recalls, litigation, investigations, and civil/criminal liability; category-wide loss of confidence can harm the business even if unrelated to its products.
- Competitive dynamics: intense competition from global peers, regional/local players, private label/economy brands, and direct-to-consumer micro brands; Coca-Cola cited as primary beverage competitor in many markets; competition based on brand strength, taste, price/value, quality, variety/innovation, distribution, marketing/promotion, packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to trends; risks if unable to promote existing products, launch/market new ones, adopt technologies (AI, data analytics), enhance digital marketing, or counter competitor spending, supply disruptions, and commodity-driven pricing pressure, potentially weakening competitive and financial position.

nodes.title: Product recalls or other issues or concerns with respect to product quality and safety can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Product recalls or other issues or concerns with respect to product quality and safety can adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: We have and could in the future recall products due to product quality or safety issues, including actual or alleged mislabeling, misbranding, spoilage, undeclared allergens, adulteration or contamination.
nodes.summary:
- Reputational and brand risks from perceived or actual shortcomings in ESG commitments (nutrition profile, diversity, equity and inclusion, packaging, water use, environmental impact), handling of health concerns about products/ingredients (including obesity), R&D outcomes, and public responses to advertising, sponsorships, social media, and social/political events; inability to counter negative commentary can reduce demand.

- Product quality and safety risks, including recalls due to mislabeling, misbranding, spoilage, undeclared allergens, adulteration or contamination—also affecting joint ventures and new categories like alcoholic beverage distribution. Consequences include inventory loss, sales disruption, increased costs, fines/judgments, litigation, investigations, potential civil/criminal liability, production/delivery disruptions, reputational damage, and broader loss of consumer confidence; underscores need for strong quality oversight.

- Competitive pressures from global players (notably The Coca‑Cola Company), regional/local brands, private label/economy brands, and smaller direct-to-consumer micro brands. Competition centers on brand loyalty, taste, price/value, quality, variety, innovation, distribution, advertising/marketing/promotions, packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to consumer trends.

- Operational and strategic requirements to remain competitive: effectively promote existing products and launch new ones; adopt technologies (including AI and data analytics) to generate insights and improve efficiency; strengthen digital marketing; and respond to supply disruptions and pricing pressure (including commodity inflation). Failure in these areas can adversely affect the business.

nodes.title: Any inability to compete effectively can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Any inability to compete ef fectively can adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Our produ cts compete against products of international beverage and convenient food companies that, like us, operate in multiple geographies, as well as regional, local and private label and economy brand manufacturers and other competitors, including smaller companies developing and selling micro brands directly to consumers through e-commerce platforms or through retailers focused on locally sourced products.
nodes.summary:
- Reputation and ESG risks: Potential harm from failing to meet environmental, social and governance goals (nutrition profile, DEI initiatives, packaging, water use, environmental impact), negative consumer perceptions of advertising, sponsorships, marketing, and responses to political/social events, and social media backlash—any of which can reduce demand.
- Product quality and safety: Risks of recalls due to mislabeling, allergens, contamination, spoilage or adulteration, including in joint ventures and new categories like alcoholic beverages; consequences include lost sales, destroyed inventory, production/distribution disruptions, fines, litigation, investigations, and lasting brand damage—even broader loss of confidence in product safety across the market.
- Competitive dynamics: Intense competition from global players (with The Coca-Cola Company as primary beverage rival), regional/local/private label brands, and direct-to-consumer micro brands; competition on brand, taste, price, quality, innovation, distribution, marketing, packaging, convenience, and responsiveness to trends; need to adopt technologies (AI, data analytics), strengthen digital marketing, and address supply disruptions and commodity inflation to protect sales and share.
- Talent and workforce: Dependence on attracting, developing, and retaining a diverse, highly skilled workforce amid labor shortages, wage inflation, higher turnover, remote-work shifts, and succession risks (including CEO); critical needs in e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics; failure can raise costs, erode institutional knowledge and competitive advantage, and harm reputation and results.
- Water scarcity: Vulnerability due to water’s role in manufacturing and raw materials; climate change and stakeholder/regulatory pressures may trigger supply chain disruptions, higher compliance and capital costs (efficiency investments), increased water prices, operational interruptions/relocations, missed water-use goals, and reputational harm.
- Evolving retail landscape: Growth of e-commerce and hard discounters requiring new partnerships and digital capabilities while maintaining traditional retail relationships; risks if these channels take share from traditional retailers or if direct-to-consumer efforts are not profitable; increasing retailer consolidation in North America, Europe, and Latin America boosts buyer power and pressures pricing, while straining smaller customers’ viability and orders.

nodes.title: Failure to attract, develop and maintain a highly skilled and diverse workforce or effectively manage changes in our workforce can have an adverse effect on our business.
nodes.heading:
Failure to attract, develop and maintain a highly skilled and diverse workforce or effectively manage changes in our
workforce can have an adverse ef fect on our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Our busin ess requires that we attract, develop and maintain a highly skilled and diverse workforce.
nodes.summary:
- Ongoing pressure to maintain or grow sales and category share, potentially requiring increased capital, marketing, and other expenditures.
- Talent and workforce risks: intense competition for skilled, diverse employees; wage inflation, labor shortages, higher turnover, remote-work shifts; succession planning (including CEO); need for e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics capabilities; potential loss of institutional knowledge, higher costs, and reputational harm if diversity goals aren’t met.
- Water scarcity risks: heavy reliance on water in operations and supply chain; climate change and stakeholder pressure driving conservation; potential for supply disruptions, higher compliance and capital costs, increased production costs, facility interruptions or relocations, failure to meet water goals, regulatory challenges, and reputational damage.
- Retail landscape shifts: growth of e-commerce and hard discounters; necessity to strengthen relationships across channels and build digital tools for retail partners; challenges in profitably expanding direct-to-consumer e-commerce; industry consolidation increasing retailer purchasing power in North America, Europe, and Latin America, which can pressure margins, weaken competitiveness, strain smaller customers, and lead to reduced or canceled orders; heightened dependence on key customers.

nodes.title: Water scarcity can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Water scarcity can adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: We and our business partners use water in the manufacturing of our products.
nodes.summary:
- Highlights risk of stagnating or declining sales and market share, potentially requiring increased capital, marketing, or other expenditures.
- Emphasizes workforce risks: intense competition for talent; wage inflation, labor shortages, higher turnover, and remote-work shifts; importance of succession planning (including CEO); and need for skills in e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics. Notes potential impacts such as loss of institutional knowledge, higher costs, reduced competitiveness, and reputational harm, including from failing to attract and develop diverse talent.
- Details water scarcity risks: dependence on water for manufacturing and raw materials; climate-change-driven scarcity; stakeholder pressures to conserve/replenish water; possible supply chain disruptions, higher compliance and capital costs (e.g., water-efficiency technologies), increased production costs, operational interruptions/relocations, failure to meet water goals, and reputational damage.
- Describes retail landscape shifts: growth of e-commerce channels and hard discounters; necessity of strong partnerships with both emerging and traditional retailers; need to build superior digital tools for retail partners and expand profitable direct-to-consumer capabilities. Warns of retail consolidation in North America, Europe, and Latin America increasing buyer power, pressuring competitiveness and margins, and straining smaller customers, which can lead to payment issues or reduced/canceled orders.

nodes.title: Changes in the retail landscape or in sales to any key customer can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Changes in the retail landscape or in sales to any key customer can adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: The retail landscape continues to evolve, including continued growth in e-commerce channels and hard discounters.
nodes.summary:
- Overall risk that failure to grow sales or category share may require increased capital, marketing, or other spending.
- Talent and workforce risks: difficulty attracting, developing, and retaining a highly skilled and diverse workforce amid wage inflation, labor shortages, higher turnover, and shifts to remote work; succession planning challenges (including CEO); need for e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics capabilities; potential reputational and performance impacts from insufficient diversity and inclusion.
- Water scarcity risks: heavy reliance on water for manufacturing and raw materials; scarcity/quality issues and stakeholder pressure can drive supply chain disruptions, higher compliance and capital costs (e.g., efficiency technologies), increased production costs, operational interruptions or relocation, inability to meet water goals, and reputational damage.
- Retail landscape changes: continued rise of e-commerce and hard discounters; need to sustain relationships across channels and build better digital tools for retailers; challenges in profitably expanding direct-to-consumer; consolidation increasing retailers’ purchasing power and pressuring margins; smaller customers’ reduced ability to compete or pay; dependence on key customers (e.g., Walmart) with risks from disputes, financial stress, reduced orders, or loss.
- Manufacturing and supply chain disruptions and cost inflation: sourcing from unstable regions; limited/sole-source materials; seasonal shortages; volatility in prices and availability of commodities, fuel, packaging (including recycled PET), transportation, and labor due to supply-demand shifts, capacity constraints, inflation, weather/climate change, natural disasters, disease/pests (e.g., citrus greening), epidemics/pandemics (including COVID-19), labor shortages/strikes (including rail), trade restrictions (tariffs, sanctions, quotas), port congestion, transport constraints, cybersecurity incidents, loss of key sites, political instability, terrorism, and currency movements. Noted higher-than-expected commodity, packaging, and transport costs in 2022; limited ability to raise prices or hedge can reduce volume, revenue, margins, and results.
- Political and social instability: elections, referendums, government shutdowns, and hostilities can alter or create uncertainty around laws and policies (tariffs, sanctions, environmental/climate rules, taxes, benefits, cross-border movement), leading to exchange rate volatility, stock market swings, global economic uncertainty, and weaker demand.

nodes.title: Disruption of our manufacturing operations or supply chain, including continued increased commodity, packaging, transportation, labor and other input costs, can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading:
Disruption of our manufacturing operations or supply chain, including continued increased commodity , packaging,
transportation, labor and other input costs, can adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: We have experience d and could continue to experience disruption in our manufa cturing operations and supply chain.
nodes.summary:
- Reliance on key retail customers (e.g., Walmart); disputes, financial deterioration, reduced purchases, or loss of such customers could materially harm the business.
- Vulnerability to manufacturing and supply chain disruptions; dependence on limited or sole-source suppliers, some in politically or economically unstable regions; contingency plans may not prevent shortages or interruptions.
- Significant volatility and potential shortages in inputs—agricultural commodities, packaging (including recycled PET), fuel, transportation, and labor—driven by supply-demand shifts, inflation, weather and climate change, natural disasters, crop diseases (e.g., citrus greening), pandemics (e.g., COVID-19), labor shortages (e.g., truck drivers), strikes (including rail), government actions (tariffs, sanctions, quotas), port congestion, capacity constraints, cybersecurity incidents, loss of key facilities, political instability, terrorism, and currency fluctuations.
- Elevated commodity, packaging, and transportation costs experienced in 2022 may persist; limited ability to raise prices or hedge could compress volume, revenue, margins, and operating results.
- Adverse impacts from political and social conditions in sales markets; elections, referendums, government shutdowns, and geopolitical hostilities can alter or create uncertainty in laws and policies (tariffs, sanctions, environmental/climate rules, taxes, benefits, cross-border movement), influence international relations and consumer perceptions, and drive exchange-rate volatility, stock market swings, global economic uncertainty, and weaker demand.

nodes.title: Political and social conditions can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Political and social conditions can adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Political and social conditions in the markets in which our products are sold have been and could continue to be difficult to predict, resulting in adverse effects on our business.
nodes.summary:
- Dependence on key customers (e.g., Walmart): disputes, financial distress, reduced purchases, or loss of a major customer could materially harm results.
- Manufacturing and supply chain risks: disruptions from supplier concentration, instability in sourcing regions, limited or seasonal availability of inputs, and the limits of contingency plans can increase costs and interrupt supply.
- Input cost inflation and volatility: agricultural commodities, fuel, packaging (including recycled PET), transportation, and labor are exposed to weather/climate change, natural disasters, crop disease (e.g., citrus greening), pandemics (including COVID-19), labor shortages (e.g., truck drivers), strikes/work stoppages (including rail), government actions (tariffs, sanctions, quotas, trade barriers), port congestion, capacity constraints, cybersecurity incidents, loss of key manufacturing sites, political instability, and currency movements. Higher-than-expected commodity, packaging, and transportation costs were experienced in 2022 and may persist; pricing or hedging may not fully offset these pressures without impacting volume, revenue, margins, or operating results.
- Political and social instability: elections, referendums, government shutdowns, international hostilities, and regulatory uncertainty (tariffs, sanctions, environmental/climate rules, taxes, movement of goods/people) can drive FX volatility, market turbulence, global economic uncertainty, and weaker demand. Protests and related government actions can disrupt operations and distribution.
- Developing and emerging markets exposure (e.g., Mexico, Middle East, China, South Africa, Brazil, India): challenges with product acceptance, competition, pricing, cultural preferences, and distribution; risks from economic/political/social conditions, war/terror/civil unrest, sanctions, foreign ownership limits, nationalization, mandated closures, trade restrictions, hyperinflation, currency devaluation/demonetization, capital controls causing trapped cash and potential deconsolidation, weak legal systems, and heightened compliance burdens (FCPA, U.K. Bribery Act, sanctions laws) with potential fines. Inability to grow or earn expected returns in these markets would adversely affect performance.
- Macroeconomic headwinds: inflation, interest rate and tax changes, recessions/slowdowns, commodity volatility, labor shortages, currency issues, credit contraction, austerity/stimulus shifts, sovereign credit deterioration, and declines in pension asset values that may raise benefit costs/funding needs; adverse impacts on financial counterparties and other partners can further affect the business.
- Cybersecurity and IT reliance: future cyber incidents or disruptions to information systems, public websites, and cloud services could adversely affect operations.

nodes.title: Our business can be adversely affected if we are unable to grow in developing and emerging markets.
nodes.heading: Our business can be adversely af fected if we are unable to grow in developing and emerging markets.
nodes.start_phrase: Our success depends in part on our ability to grow our business in developing and emer ging markets, including Mexico, the Middle East, China, South Africa, Brazil and India.
nodes.summary:
- Highlights risks from political and social unrest, demonstrations, and government actions in U.S. and global cities that can disrupt operations, distribution, and supply of ingredients/raw materials.
- Details challenges of expanding in developing and emerging markets (e.g., Mexico, Middle East, China, South Africa, Brazil, India), including product acceptance, competition, cultural differences, distribution methods, and regulatory, political, and economic instability.
- Enumerates specific international risks: tariffs and sanctions, foreign ownership limits, nationalization, mandated closures, import/export restrictions, high inflation, currency devaluation/controls/demonetization, cash trapping and potential deconsolidation, weak legal systems, and heightened compliance burdens (e.g., FCPA, U.K. Bribery Act), including potential fines and penalties.
- Describes adverse impacts from broader economic conditions: high inflation, changing interest rates and taxes, recessions/slowdowns, commodity price volatility, labor shortages, credit contraction, austerity/stimulus effects, sovereign credit risks, and declines in pension/post-retirement asset values increasing costs and funding needs.
- Notes reliance on information systems, public websites, and cloud services, and the risk that cyber incidents or IT disruptions could impair key business activities.

nodes.title: Changes in economic conditions can adversely impact our business.
nodes.heading: Changes in economic conditions can adversely impact our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Many of the jurisdictions in which our products are sold have experienced and could continue to experience uncertain or unfavorable econom ic conditions, such as high inflation and adverse changes in interest rates, tax laws or tax rates, which could result in recessions or economic slowdowns;
nodes.summary:
- Political and social unrest in U.S. cities and globally—linked to elections, civil rights, and protests—can disrupt operations, supply chains, and distribution, including via government-mandated closures, adversely affecting the business.
- Risks and challenges in developing and emerging markets (e.g., Mexico, Middle East, China, South Africa, Brazil, India): uncertain product acceptance, strong competition, cultural and distribution differences, tariffs and sanctions, foreign ownership limits, potential nationalization, operational shutdowns, trade restrictions, high inflation, currency devaluation/demonetization, currency controls leading to trapped cash and possible deconsolidation, weak legal systems, and complex compliance with anti-corruption and trade laws (e.g., FCPA, U.K. Bribery Act), with potential fines and penalties; risk of not achieving expected returns.
- Adverse macroeconomic conditions: high inflation, changes in interest rates and taxes, recessions/slowdowns, commodity price volatility, labor shortages, tight credit, sovereign credit risk, and pension asset declines increasing benefit costs and funding needs; potential knock-on effects from stressed business partners and financial institutions.
- Dependence on information systems, public websites, and cloud services exposes the company to cyber incidents and IT disruptions that could impair critical operations and communications.

nodes.title: Future cyber incidents and other disruptions to our information systems can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Future cyber incidents and other disruptions to our information systems can adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: We depen d on information systems and technology , including public websites and cloud-based services, for many activities important to our business, including communications within our company ,
nodes.summary:
- Impact of political and social unrest on operations: disruptions to production, distribution, and supply chains due to demonstrations, protests, and government actions in the U.S. and globally.
- Risks of expanding in developing and emerging markets (e.g., Mexico, Middle East, China, South Africa, Brazil, India): uncertain product acceptance, intense competition, cultural differences, regulatory barriers (tariffs, sanctions, foreign ownership limits), nationalization, forced closures, import/export restrictions, inflation, currency devaluation/demonetization/controls, legal system weaknesses, compliance burdens (FCPA, U.K. Bribery Act), potential fines, trapped cash and possible deconsolidations, and challenges achieving expected returns.
- Adverse effects of macroeconomic conditions: high inflation, interest rate and tax changes, recessions, commodity volatility, labor shortages, currency instability, credit contraction, sovereign credit issues, and pension asset declines; knock-on impacts from weakened business partners and financial institutions.
- Cybersecurity and IT disruptions: dependence on information systems; increasing frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks (ransomware, DDoS, social engineering, supply-chain exploits, credential theft, crypto mining, BEC); heightened remote-work vulnerabilities; potential consequences include operational shutdowns, data/IP loss, financial losses, litigation, regulatory actions, reputational harm, and customer loss; similar risks in acquired entities, JVs, and partners.
- Third-party and supply-chain IT risks: vulnerabilities from suppliers and cloud/software providers, including malware introduced via updates; coordination challenges that can amplify incident impact even without a direct breach.
- Insurance limitations: cyber insurance may not cover all losses, claim types, or reputational damage.
- Strategic transactions risks: uncertainties realizing synergies, savings, and approvals; integration/separation of operations and IT; operating in new models/territories; retaining key talent; aligning controls and compliance (financial reporting, disclosure, data protection, cybersecurity, environmental, health and safety, anti-bribery); customer retention; tax inefficiencies; dependence on JV partners; contingent liabilities and litigation; revenue loss from divestitures.
- Reliance on third-party service providers (payroll, benefits, finance/accounting): potential for errors, disruptions, data loss, incorrect financial reporting, litigation, regulatory penalties, remediation costs, reputational harm, and morale issues.
- Enterprise-wide systems transformation (ERP/finance systems): multi-year migration causing potential outages and inefficiencies; risk of not allocating sufficient resources or realizing expected benefits, adversely affecting the business.

nodes.title: Failure to successfully complete or manage strategic transactions can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Failure to successfully complete or manage strategic transactions can adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: We regula rly review our portfolio of businesses and evaluate potential acquisitions, joint ventures, distribution agreements, divestitures, refranchisings and other strategic transactions.
nodes.summary:
- Highlights cyber and information systems risks, noting that while the company maintains cybersecurity insurance, coverage may not address all losses, claims, or reputational damage from incidents.
- Details risks tied to strategic transactions (acquisitions, joint ventures, distribution agreements, divestitures, refranchising), including challenges with integrating or separating operations and IT, entering new models or markets, talent retention, aligning controls and compliance (financial reporting, data protection, cybersecurity, environmental, health and safety, anti-bribery), customer retention, tax inefficiencies, relations with divested or refranchised entities, revenue loss, joint venture misalignment, and unforeseen liabilities or litigation. Notes prior adverse effects when transactions were not effectively managed.
- Describes dependence on third-party service providers (including cloud) for payroll, benefits, and finance/accounting, where failures or poor oversight can lead to added costs, disruptions, system degradation, processing inefficiencies, IP or data loss, security breaches, inaccurate financial reporting, legal/regulatory actions, fines, remediation costs, reputational harm, and negative employee morale.
- Explains risks from a multi-year migration to enterprise-wide systems (including financial systems), with reported and potential outages and inefficiencies post-implementation; emphasizes the need for adequate IT resourcing and warns that failing to achieve expected benefits could adversely affect the business.
- Overall, underscores potential operational, financial, regulatory, and reputational impacts if these risks materialize or are not effectively managed.

nodes.title: Our reliance on third-party service providers and enterprise-wide systems can have an adverse effect on our business.
nodes.heading: Our reliance on third-party service providers and enterprise-wide systems can have an adverse ef fect on our business.
nodes.start_phrase: We rely on third-pa rty service providers, including cloud data service provid ers, for certain areas of our business, including payroll processing, health and benefit plan administration and certain finance and accounting functions.
nodes.summary:
- Limits of cyber incident insurance: Coverage may not fully address losses, claim types, or reputational damage from cyber events and systems failures.
- Strategic transaction risks: Challenges in executing and integrating or separating acquisitions, joint ventures, divestitures, and refranchisings; risks include failure to realize synergies, systems and process integration, operating in new models/markets, talent retention, aligning controls and compliance (financial reporting, disclosure, data protection, cybersecurity, environmental, health and safety, anti-bribery), customer retention, tax inefficiencies, JV partner misalignment, contingent liabilities and litigation.
- Reliance on third-party service providers: Outsourcing (e.g., cloud, payroll, benefits, finance/accounting) can lead to errors, disruptions, degraded performance, data loss/security breaches, financial reporting issues, regulatory actions, fines, remediation costs, litigation, reputational damage, and morale impacts if providers fail or are poorly monitored.
- Enterprise systems transformation: Multi-year migration to enterprise-wide solutions (including finance) has caused and may continue to cause outages and inefficiencies; inadequate IT resourcing or failure to achieve expected benefits could adversely affect the business.
- Climate change impacts: Physical risks to facilities and supply chain from extreme weather; agricultural yield and commodity cost/availability pressures (e.g., potatoes, sugar cane, corn, wheat, rice, oats, oranges); expanding regulations (GHG, carbon pricing, labeling, single-use plastics) increasing costs and required investments; reputational and demand risks from failure to meet or report sustainability goals; potential litigation.
- Labor relations: High unionization and reliance on third parties with unionized workforces create risks of strikes or work stoppages that can disrupt manufacturing and distribution, interrupt supply, reduce sales, raise costs, and hinder operational changes.
- Financial performance risks from productivity initiatives: Efforts (e.g., shared services) may not deliver anticipated savings and can cause disruptions, management/employee distraction, morale declines, attrition, talent attraction/retention challenges, and negative publicity.
- Impairment risk: Deterioration in business performance estimates or assumptions can lead to goodwill and intangible asset impairment charges, adversely affecting results.

nodes.title: Climate change or measures to address climate change can negatively affect our business or damage our reputation.
nodes.heading: Climate change or measures to address climate change can negatively af fect our business or damage our reputation.
nodes.start_phrase: Climate change may increase the frequency or severity of natural disasters and other extreme weather conditions (including rising temperatures and drought), which could pose physical risks to our facilities, impair our production capabilities, disrupt our supply chain or impact demand for our product s.
nodes.summary:
- Climate change risks: Increased frequency/severity of extreme weather and physical risks to facilities; disruptions to production, supply chains, and product demand; adverse impacts on availability and pricing of key agricultural commodities (e.g., potatoes, sugar cane, corn, wheat, rice, oats, oranges); growing regulatory pressures (GHG emissions, energy policy, single-use plastics, carbon pricing, labeling) leading to higher costs and capital needs; reputational and litigation risks tied to sustainability performance and reporting.

- Labor relations risks: Dependence on workforces covered by collective bargaining agreements, with potential for strikes, work stoppages, or other disruptions that could impede manufacturing and distribution, reduce sales, increase costs, and hinder operational changes.

- Financial risks from productivity initiatives: Reliance on cost-reduction and efficiency programs (including multi-year shared business services) that may cause unintended consequences—business disruption, management distraction, lower morale and productivity, unexpected attrition, talent attraction/retention challenges, and negative publicity—leading to failure to achieve anticipated savings and weaker financial performance.

- Impairment risk: Potential for impairment charges if estimates and assumptions about future performance deteriorate, affecting goodwill and other indefinite-lived intangible assets (with the discussion on amortizable assets cut off).

nodes.title: Strikes or work stoppages can cause our business to suffer.
nodes.heading: Strikes or work stoppages can cause our business to suf fer.
nodes.start_phrase: Many of our employ ees and employees of third parties that are involved in the manufacturing, production or distribution of our products are covered by collective bargaining agreements, and other employees may seek to be covered by collective bargaining agreements.
nodes.summary:
- Climate change risks: Physical impacts from extreme weather, rising temperatures, and drought could disrupt facilities, production, supply chains, and product demand.
- Raw material exposure: Agricultural volatility may reduce availability or raise costs of key commodities (e.g., potatoes, sugar cane, corn, wheat, rice, oats, oranges).
- Regulatory and sustainability pressures: Growing climate-related regulations (e.g., greenhouse gas controls, carbon pricing, energy policies, single-use plastics, labeling) and sustainability initiatives may increase costs and require additional capital investments.
- Reputation and litigation risk: Failure to meet or transparently report environmental goals, or perceptions of irresponsible environmental practices, could trigger adverse publicity, reduced demand, reputational harm, and higher litigation risk.
- Labor relations risk: Strikes or work stoppages involving employees or third parties under collective bargaining agreements could disrupt manufacturing and distribution, interrupt supply, increase costs, reduce sales, and impede operational changes.
